subChunks.title: Tailwind Config Deep-Dive
subChunks.hookHtml: Tailwind v4 replaced tailwind.config.js with a CSS-first configuration system. Your design tokens live in CSS, not JavaScript — and everything you define automatically becomes a Tailwind utility. This is where a generic framework becomes your design system.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon: "In the old days, apprentices wrestled with JavaScript config files. Tailwind v4 put the tokens where they belong — in CSS itself. The system is simpler and far more powerful. Sit. We begin."

@theme — the constitution

Every token you define in an @theme block becomes a CSS variable and a Tailwind utility automatically. Define a colour once, get bg-brand, text-brand, border-brand, and every other variant for free.

/* index.css */
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  /* Colors */
  --color-brand:     oklch(0.55 0.20 270);   /* bg-brand, text-brand, etc. */
  --color-brand-600: oklch(0.55 0.20 270);

  /* Typography */
  --font-display: "Cal Sans", sans-serif;    /* font-display */

  /* Spacing */
  --spacing-18: 4.5rem;   /* p-18, m-18, w-18, gap-18 */

  /* Breakpoints */
  --breakpoint-xs:  480px;   /* xs:text-sm, xs:flex, etc. */
  --breakpoint-3xl: 1920px;

  /* Radius & shadow */
  --radius-4xl: 2rem;
  --shadow-glow: 0 0 20px 4px oklch(0.55 0.2 270 / 0.4);
}

The naming convention is always --{category}-{name}. Tailwind reads the category to know which utilities to generate. --color-* → colour utilities. --spacing-* → spacing utilities.

The semantic token pattern

@import "tailwindcss";
@variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));

@theme {
  --color-primary:            var(--color-brand-600);
  --color-primary-foreground: oklch(0.99 0 0);
  --color-surface:            oklch(0.99 0 0);
}

/* Dark mode overrides the same variable names */
.dark {
  --color-primary:  var(--color-brand-400);
  --color-surface:  oklch(0.12 0 0);
}

Custom utilities: @utility

@utility scrollbar-hide {
  -ms-overflow-style: none;
  scrollbar-width: none;
  &::-webkit-scrollbar { display: none; }
}

/* Usage — participates in variants */
<div class="scrollbar-hide overflow-y-auto">

Custom variants: @variant

@variant scrolled (&:where(.scrolled, .scrolled *));
@variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));
@variant rtl ([dir=rtl] &);

<nav class="bg-transparent scrolled:bg-white/90 scrolled:shadow-sm">

v3 → v4 quick reference

v3 tailwind.config.js                →  v4 CSS equivalent
theme.extend.colors.brand: '#...'    →  @theme { --color-brand: oklch(...); }
theme.extend.spacing[18]: '4.5rem'  →  @theme { --spacing-18: 4.5rem; }
darkMode: 'class'                    →  @variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));
addUtilities({ .foo: { ... } })      →  @utility foo { ... }

Solomon: "The config is not a file you set once and forget. It is where every design commitment is recorded — in the same language as the rest of your styles."

storyBeats.text: The Grand Archmage's study is quiet except for the scratch of his quill. He does not look up when you enter — but a CSS file slides across the desk toward you. There is no tailwind.config.js anywhere in the room.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: Tailwind v4 moved the configuration into CSS where it belongs. Every token you declare in @theme becomes a CSS variable and a Tailwind utility simultaneously. Name it once, use it everywhere.

storyBeats.speaker: @theme — token becomes utility automatically

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a branded card that demonstrates the semantic token pattern:

  • .branded-card: bg-indigo-50, border, border-indigo-200, rounded-xl, p-6
  • .branded-heading: text-indigo-900, text-xl, font-bold, mb-2
  • .branded-badge: bg-indigo-600, text-white, text-xs, font-semibold, px-2.5, py-0.5, rounded-full
  • .branded-body: text-indigo-700, text-sm, leading-relaxed
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
Arcane Config

Expert

Design tokens centralise every colour decision so a rebrand is a config change, not a file search.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a brand token showcase card from scratch using only custom semantic classes you define yourself (e.g. .bg-brand-primary, .text-brand-accent). Apply them to a card with a title, body text, and a CTA button — no pre-defined utility class list given.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Tailwind v4 @theme block to a developer who only knows the v3 tailwind.config.js approach. Cover: how a token defined in @theme becomes a utility, how to handle semantic tokens for dark mode and theming, and the v3→v4 translation for colours, spacing, and dark mode configuration.

questions.prompt: In Tailwind v4, where does configuration live — and what format does it take?
options: In your CSS file, inside an @theme {} block using CSS custom property syntax
In tailwind.config.js using a JavaScript export default object
In a .tailwindrc JSON file at the project root
questions.answer: In your CSS file, inside an @theme {} block using CSS custom property syntax
questions.explanation: Tailwind v4 moved to CSS-first configuration. You define tokens inside @theme { --color-brand: ...; --spacing-18: 4.5rem; } in your CSS file. There is no tailwind.config.js. The naming convention --{category}-{name} tells Tailwind which utilities to generate.

questions.prompt: You add --color-brand-600: oklch(0.55 0.20 270) to your @theme block. Which Tailwind utilities are automatically generated?
options: bg-brand-600, text-brand-600, border-brand-600, ring-brand-600 — and every other colour utility variant
Only bg-brand-600 — other utilities require separate declarations
bg-brand-600 and text-brand-600 only — border utilities need explicit config
A CSS variable is created but no utility is generated automatically
questions.answer: bg-brand-600, text-brand-600, border-brand-600, ring-brand-600 — and every other colour utility variant
questions.explanation: Every token in @theme automatically generates the full utility lattice for its category. A --color-* token becomes bg-*, text-*, border-*, ring-*, fill-*, stroke-*, and every other colour utility — plus opacity modifier support (e.g. bg-brand-600/50) for free.

questions.prompt: A startup built their product using raw colour utilities (text-indigo-600, bg-indigo-500) across 300 files. Marketing wants the brand colour changed to teal. What architectural choice would have made this a 5-minute change?
options: Semantic tokens: define --color-brand-600 in @theme, use bg-brand-600 everywhere — a rebrand is then one variable change
Use CSS custom properties directly: var(--brand) — no Tailwind utilities needed
Use @apply with a .brand-bg class throughout — then change the one class definition
Find-and-replace all indigo references at once — it is a quick operation in a modern IDE
questions.answer: Semantic tokens: define --color-brand-600 in @theme, use bg-brand-600 everywhere — a rebrand is then one variable change
questions.explanation: Without semantic tokens, every indigo class could mean 'brand' or 'decorative' — there is no way to tell. A find-and-replace will miss some and break others. With @theme { --color-brand-600: oklch(...); } and bg-brand-600 throughout, a rebrand is a single variable change. This is the core value of the semantic token pattern.
